How to Choose a Water Filter

What to check before you buy — from the CDC

Most people do not need a complicated system. They need to match the filter to the water they have.

The CDC says the most common home pitchers and fridge filters are not designed to remove germs. They improve taste and smell only. They do not make bad water safe.

Before you buy, check the label for:

  • Parasites (Giardia, Cryptosporidium): an absolute pore size of 1 micron or smaller, or NSF 53 or 58 cyst certification.
  • Bacteria (Salmonella, E. coli): an absolute pore size of 0.3 micron or smaller, or ultrafiltration, nanofiltration, or reverse osmosis.
  • Viruses: portable filters do NOT remove viruses. You need boiling, disinfection, or a full treatment system for viruses.

Absolute vs. mean pore size

Absolute pore size: every pore is 1 micron or smaller. Anything larger is caught. This is what the CDC means by "1 micron or smaller."

Mean (nominal) pore size: the average pore size. Some pores are smaller, some are larger. A "mean 1 micron" filter may let 1-micron germs through.

What to look for on the label

Look for an NSF International certification number. The CDC notes NSF Standard 53 for cyst reduction and NSF Standard 58 for reverse osmosis. These are independent public health standards.

Source

CDC — "About Choosing Home Water Filters," https://www.cdc.gov/drinking-water/prevention/about-choosing-home-water-filters.html
